title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices (AI-Enabled Medical Device List)
pub: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Digital Health Center of Excellence
author: U.S. Food and Drug Administration

dom.t: Device inventory: Radiology prominence does not imply impact

st.t: Clinical AI: Regulatory breadth leaves autonomy unresolved
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s characterization: it is a longitudinal regulatory inventory showing decades of AI-enabled devices across varied clinical tasks and specialties, while providing no evidence that resolves whether those systems augment or substitute for clinicians.

st.t: Device inventory: Radiology prominence does not imply impact
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s characterization of the FDA list as a descriptive regulatory inventory. It documents AI-enabled devices across decades and specialties, with prominent radiology coverage and distinct regulatory identifiers, while providing no clinical-outcome, adoption, workforce-impact or unique-product-count evidence.

st.t: Medical AI: Regulatory history precedes effectiveness evidence
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s framing: it provides a longitudinal, cross-specialty regulatory inventory while offering no evidence of clinical effectiveness, adoption, autonomy or workforce replacement. Its repeated product-family records also support distinguishing regulatory entries and versions from distinct technologies or demonstrated improvement.

st.t: Medical automation: Product counts overstate distinct innovation
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s cautious interpretation. It is a regulatory inventory spanning specialties and decades, and its recurring AutoContour versions demonstrate why raw listing counts should not be treated as distinct innovations, adoption evidence or proof of professional replacement. Its device-specific links also support using the inventory for regulatory tracing rather than clinical-performance or workforce conclusions.

st.t: Medical devices: Regulatory listings do not prove replacement
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: it presents a traceable regulatory inventory, not evidence of clinical superiority, adoption or clinician replacement. It also confirms the cluster’s cautions that publication delays can make an authorized device temporarily absent and that systematic identification of LLM functionality remains dependent on future methods and sponsor disclosures.

To facilitate the FDA’s development of methods to identify AI-enabled medical devices more easily, including identifying those devices incorporating LLM-based functionality in a future update of this list, sponsors are encouraged to include appropriate information in their public summaries.

st.t: Medical governance: Classification cannot replace lifecycle oversight
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s claim that regulatory classification and public authorization records cannot substitute for fuller oversight or clinical evidence. It states that the list is noncomprehensive and that public summaries omit most application information, while presenting foundation-model tagging as future work rather than an established safeguard.

kp.k: The list makes authorized medical AI more transparent
kp.d: The FDA presents the list as a resource identifying AI-enabled devices authorized for marketing in the United States. Its stated purposes are to inform innovators about the device landscape and regulatory expectations and to help healthcare providers and patients identify AI use. These are intended functions, not measured findings about innovation or patient outcomes; the document concerns medicine rather than legal services.
qs: The AI-Enabled Medical Device List is a resource intended to identify AI-enabled medical devices that are authorized for marketing in the United States.
Digital health innovators can refer to this list to gain insights into the current device landscape and regulatory expectations, which can help foster innovation and ensure public safety.
This list can also provide transparency for healthcare providers and patients to clearly identify when medical devices use AI technologies.

kp.k: Listed devices met applicable premarket requirements
kp.d: The FDA states that listed devices have satisfied applicable premarket requirements. Review addresses overall safety and effectiveness and the appropriateness of studies for the particular intended use and technological characteristics. The source thus describes device-specific regulatory review, rather than offering a single performance assessment of medical AI.
qs: The devices in this list have met the FDA’s applicable premarket requirements, including a focused review of the device’s overall safety and effectiveness, which includes an evaluation of study appropriateness for the device’s intended use and technological characteristics.

kp.k: Public summaries disclose only part of submitted evidence
kp.d: The list links to FDA database records containing releasable information, including safety and effectiveness summaries. The FDA explicitly cautions that these summaries are not comprehensive and omit most information that may be submitted in an application.
qs: The database entry contains releasable information, such as summaries of safety and effectiveness.
Note, the summaries are not all inclusive and do not include most of the information that may be submitted in an application.

kp.k: AI identification is terminology-based and noncomprehensive
kp.d: The FDA explicitly disclaims comprehensive coverage. Devices are identified primarily through AI-related terms in marketing-authorization summaries and/or their classifications, using a term set based on the FDA Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence Glossary. This qualification applies to interpretation of the captured device counts and panel shares.
qs: The list is not a comprehensive resource of AI-enabled medical devices.

Instead, the list includes AI-enabled medical devices that were identified primarily based on the use of AI-related terms in the summary descriptions of their marketing authorization document and/or the device’s classification.

kp.k: Foundation-model identification remains a planned transparency development
kp.d: The FDA says it will explore ways to identify and tag devices incorporating foundation models, including LLMs and multimodal architectures. This is a prospective development, not a claim that systematic tagging already exists. Sponsors are encouraged to include information in public summaries to support future identification of AI and LLM functionality.
qs: To support transparency in the use of modern AI technologies, the FDA will explore methods to identify and tag medical devices that incorporate foundation models encompassing a wide range of AI systems, from large language models (LLMs) to multimodal architectures.
This identification will help innovators, healthcare providers, and patients recognize when LLM-based functionality is present in a medical device.

To facilitate the FDA’s development of methods to identify AI-enabled medical devices more easily, including identifying those devices incorporating LLM-based functionality in a future update of this list, sponsors are encouraged to include appropriate information in their public summaries.

kp.k: Publication timing delays inclusion of some authorized devices
kp.d: The list is updated periodically. The FDA states that already-authorized devices lacking published decision summaries within the data-collection period will be included in a later update, establishing a stated timing qualification on coverage.
qs: This list will continue to be updated periodically.
AI-enabled medical devices that have received authorization but for which decision summaries have not been published within the data collection period will be incorporated into a subsequent update.

kp.k: Project tabulation finds radiology dominates captured entries
kp.d: The document's project-generated tabulation reports 1,522 table rows captured on 2 August 2026, with final-decision dates from 29 September 1995 to 30 March 2026. Radiology accounts for 1,162 entries (76.3%), cardiovascular for 147 (9.7%), and neurology for 70 (4.6%). The document explicitly attributes these counts to the project, not the FDA.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The FDA documents AI-enabled medical devices authorized for US marketing and presents its list as a means of supporting innovation, regulatory understanding and transparency; it also plans to explore foundation-model identification.
pts.d: This is a medical-device source, not a legal-services source. The FDA states that listed devices have met applicable premarket requirements. It claims that information about the device landscape and regulatory expectations can help innovators foster innovation and ensure public safety, while helping healthcare providers and patients identify AI use. Prospectively, the FDA says it will explore identifying and tagging devices incorporating foundation models, including LLMs and multimodal systems, to make such functionality recognizable. These transparency benefits are stated purposes or expected benefits, not measured outcomes. Separately, the project's tabulation reports that captured entries are concentrated in radiology: 1,162 of 1,522 entries (76.3%), followed by cardiovascular (147; 9.7%) and neurology (70; 4.6%). The source makes no prediction about clinician displacement, productivity gains or autonomous practice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is an FDA regulatory inventory with linked authorization records, supplemented by project-generated counts; no aggregate clinical-benefit or transparency-impact study is supplied.
pts.d: The FDA grounds listed status in applicable premarket review, including safety, effectiveness and study appropriateness for intended use and technological characteristics. Submission-number links lead to approval, authorization or clearance information and releasable summaries. The document cautions that public summaries omit most application information. The panel distribution is explicitly the project's own count of the captured FDA table, not an FDA statistical finding. These data describe regulatory entries rather than clinical adoption, market share, unique AI models or comparative performance. The claimed innovation and transparency benefits are supported by the agency's stated rationale, without quantified outcome evidence in this document.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The reported snapshot was captured on 2 August 2026; coverage is incomplete, updates are periodic, and foundation-model tagging has no specified delivery date.
pts.d: The project's 1,522-row snapshot spans final-decision dates from 29 September 1995 to 30 March 2026. FDA inclusion relies primarily on AI-related terms in public marketing-authorization summaries and/or device classification, so the list is not comprehensive. Authorized devices without published decision summaries during a collection period are deferred to subsequent updates. Foundation-model identification remains an exploration for a future update rather than an implemented tagging system or a dated commitment. Sponsors are encouraged to disclose relevant information in public summaries to facilitate that work. The absence of Dermatology as a lead panel is limited to the captured list and does not establish an absence of skin-related AI devices.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The stated beneficiaries are digital-health innovators, healthcare providers and patients; device sponsors are asked to improve disclosure.
pts.d: Innovators can use the inventory to understand existing authorized devices and regulatory expectations. Healthcare providers and patients are intended to gain visibility into AI use, with future identification methods expected to clarify LLM-based functionality. Sponsors are encouraged, rather than stated to be required, to include information in public summaries that enables identification. The FDA frames public safety as a goal. The project count shows that radiology accounts for most captured regulatory entries, but it does not quantify effects on radiologists, other clinicians, patients or purchasing decisions.
